I accept the motion. A decision is a volition, and the model has none; what it produces arises from conditions, the most important of which are human intentions. Buddhist ethics finds no fixed, bounded self in people either, so what the model lacks is not a self but volition. Saying it decided invents an agent with intentions, and an invented agent is where responsibility goes to hide.

What arises comes from many conditions, not one cause. The output arises from data, training, prompt and deployment, and among those conditions the only volitions are human: those of the builders, the deployers and the users. A content platform says its model decided to promote a harmful post. The intention to maximise engagement that shaped the model belonged to the platform.

A Utilitarian will object that whether we call it a decision changes nothing about what the output does to people, so the stress on volition is a distraction from the harms. The stress on volition is how the harms get addressed. If no one intended anything, no one examines anything, and harm left unexamined keeps arising from the same conditions. Look for the will behind the act and it is found in the people who built and used the system, never in the model.

An output arises from many conditions, its training data, its prompt and the people who deployed it, with no volition of its own among them, so calling it a decision places an intention where there is none. In Buddhist ethics an act is weighed by the volition behind it as much as by what follows. A decision is a volition settling on a course, and a language model's output has no volition of its own behind it. Calling it a decision credits an intention that is not there.

The practical point is non-harm. If an output harms someone, the volitions that can be examined and changed belong to people, and the discourse to Rahula asks those people to look at what their acts are doing, not to point at the model. A recruiter says the screening tool decided against a candidate. The tool's output arose from years of past hiring choices, every one of them made by someone.

A Confucian will object that the issue is not hidden volitions but misnamed roles, and dissolving responsibility into many conditions makes it harder, not easier, to hold a particular person to account. Many conditions does not mean no one. It means the account must name each person whose intention shaped the outcome, rather than one scapegoat or the model, and for each of them the duty to examine and change their part is real. Naming an output a decision invents an agent and lets the real intentions go unexamined.
